prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules, and they should do it soon. The case does not rest on hostility to cars or on any wish to punish drivers. It rests on a simple observation: a city that dictates how much parking every building must contain is making a private business decision on behalf of thousands of people it has never met, and it has been getting that decision wrong for decades.

Minimum parking requirements began in the mid-twentieth century as a well-meaning attempt to keep curbs from overflowing. Planners looked at manuals that estimated parking demand and wrote those estimates into zoning codes as legal floors. The trouble is that the estimates were crude, often based on a handful of suburban sites with free parking and no transit, and they were then applied to everything from corner cafes to downtown apartments. A restaurant might be told to provide one space for every hundred square feet, a flat to provide two spaces per unit, and a shop whatever the code's formula happened to dictate. The numbers sounded precise, but they were guesses dressed as rules.

The most immediate cost is to housing. A single structured parking space can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and underground spaces cost far more. Those costs do not vanish; they are passed on to tenants and buyers, including the many households that own no car at all. A renter who bikes to work ends up paying for a garage space she never uses, and a developer who might have built twenty modest homes on a lot builds twelve because the rest of the land must be paved. In a country that complains constantly about housing shortages, it is strange that we legally require builders to devote their scarcest resource to storing vehicles.

The second cost is to the shape of the city itself. Parking mandates spread buildings apart, because every shop and office must sit behind or beside a lake of asphalt. Walking from one door to the next becomes a trek across a hostile expanse, which makes driving feel necessary, which in turn justifies more parking. Older neighborhoods that grew before these rules are often the ones people love most, with their close-set storefronts and walkable blocks, and in many places those buildings could not legally be built today. We have effectively outlawed the kind of urban fabric that we then pay a premium to visit on vacation.

The third cost falls on small businesses and on the reuse of old buildings. A family that wants to turn a vacant storefront into a bakery may discover that the change of use triggers a parking requirement the lot cannot satisfy, and so the building stays empty. Entrepreneurs with limited capital are the ones least able to absorb the expense of extra spaces or the legal fees of seeking a variance. Large chains with deep pockets and standard suburban designs are the ones the rules quietly favor.

Defenders of the requirements raise a reasonable worry, which is that without mandates, new buildings will push their cars onto neighboring streets and make life miserable for existing residents. This concern deserves a real answer, and the answer is that the remedy is better management of the curb rather than a mandate on every private lot. Cities can price on-street parking so that spaces turn over and are usually available, and they can issue residential permits for neighborhoods that need protection. Revenue from meters can even be returned to the district for sidewalks and lighting, which gives residents a stake in the arrangement. Pricing addresses scarcity directly, while mandates merely hide it by supplying free parking that someone else is paying for.

It also helps to remember what removal actually means. Repealing minimums does not ban parking, and it does not force anyone to build without it. Developers who believe their tenants want spaces will keep providing them, because a building that is hard to rent is a bad investment. What changes is that the amount of parking becomes a choice informed by the market, by lenders, and by the particular block, instead of a number lifted from a manual. Some projects will build more than the old code demanded, and many will build less. That variety is exactly the point.

The evidence from cities that have tried this is encouraging. Places that have scrapped or sharply reduced their mandates, including Buenos Aires, Minneapolis, Buffalo, and a growing list of others, have not descended into gridlock or chaos. Developers there have generally continued to build parking where it makes commercial sense, while also delivering projects that would previously have been impossible. Early studies suggest that builders respond by adding homes and by trimming unneeded spaces, which is the outcome reformers hoped for.

None of this requires believing that cars are evil or that everyone should give them up. Many people will keep driving, and many neighborhoods will always need generous parking. The argument is only that a city government is a poor judge of how many spaces a particular building needs, and that the penalty for judging wrong is paid by renters, by entrepreneurs, and by the public realm. When a rule imposes large costs, rests on weak evidence, and can be replaced by a more precise tool, the sensible response is to repeal it. Cities should take the mandates off the books and let the people who build, live in, and run these places decide how much parking they truly need.
